strengths: Clear and well-formalized framework for data provenance auditing under black-box access, featuring a provable false-positive rate (FPR $\le k/K$) bound via counterfactual watermark ranking.

The cue-reply architecture embedded entirely in invisible Unicode characters provides true visible text-preservation, ensuring original literary or sensitive texts are byte-for-byte identical in rendering.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two open-weight LLMs (LLaMA-2-7B and Mistral-7B) exploring collection size, training set size scaling, and multi-watermark interference.
Thorough discussion of ethical considerations, legal context (e.g., EU AI Act, US copyright litigation), and transparent acknowledgment of core limitations.
weaknesses: Practical robustness is fragile: standard data preprocessing and web-scraping sanitization pipelines (e.g., in Dolma, FineWeb) routinely filter out zero-width and non-rendering Unicode characters (such as U+200B through U+200D and U+2060). Any basic regex-based text cleaner trivially neutralizes the watermark without visibly degrading text quality.

The evaluation is restricted to adapter-based (LoRA) fine-tuning on relatively small corpora (up to 15,000 documents) and at most 12 concurrent watermarks, leaving full parameter fine-tuning, instruction tuning, and pretraining regimes unverified.

Algorithm 1 appears to contain minor notation inconsistencies or typographical bugs (e.g., line 7 increments the chunk offset $x$ by $\lambda$, which represents the verification repetition count, rather than chunk length $\delta$).

Audit probing relies on submitting the exact odd chunk containing the cue syllables, which assumes the auditor has access to the precise original chunking structure and can submit large cue-laden text prompts to the model.

strengths: Important problem formulation: Auditing data provenance and copyright infringement in black-box LLMs without modifying visible text is a highly relevant, timely, and practical research direction.

Text-preserving design: Leveraging invisible Unicode characters ensures byte-level preservation of rendered surface text, which is especially valuable for sensitive literary domains like poetry and journalism where visible text alterations are unacceptable.

Sound statistical grounding: Combining the cue-reply canary design with a ranking test over held-out counterfactual watermarks provides an analytically bounded false-positive rate (FPR <= k/K), avoiding ad-hoc score thresholding.

Systematic empirical investigation: The paper conducts experiments across two distinct open-weight models (LLaMA-2-7B and Mistral-7B) and two datasets, evaluating key factors such as training set scaling, watermark density, and multi-watermark attribution interference.
weaknesses: High vulnerability to standard text preprocessing: Zero-width Unicode characters (U+200B, U+200C, U+200D, U+2060) are routinely removed by standard data-cleaning, deduplication, and normalization pipelines (e.g., regex stripping non-printable characters or applying Unicode normalization). While acknowledged in Section V, this fundamental fragility poses a severe practical limitation against even non-adversarial model trainers.

Restricted experimental scope: The evaluation is limited strictly to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA with r=12) over small corpora (1k to 15k instances) with relatively dense insertions (approx. one watermark per 32 tokens). It remains unverified whether detection remains effective under full fine-tuning, lower watermark densities, or pre-training regimes.

Tokenizer dependency: The method relies heavily on how tokenizers treat specific invisible code points (e.g., mapping individual zero-width characters to single distinct tokens or specific byte-fallback tokens). Modern tokenizers (such as Tiktoken or Byte-level BPE in newer models like Gemma or Llama 3) may handle invisible characters differently or group them unpredictably.

Reliance on a centralized Trusted Third Party (TTP): The attribution and ranking guarantee relies on an honest TTP to enforce uniqueness, allocate candidate sets, and commit to counterfactuals, introducing operational and trust bottlenecks in distributed auditing settings.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly timely and important problem: post-hoc, black-box auditing of training data provenance in fine-tuned LLMs without corrupting visible text.
The cue-reply architecture paired with invisible Unicode characters neatly avoids semantic and stylistic degradation of sensitive texts (e.g., poetry, literary works).
The verification protocol is grounded in a ranking test against counterfactual canaries, providing an explicit, provable upper bound on the false-positive rate (FPR <= k/K).
The paper is well-written and clearly structured, with comprehensive pseudocode (Algorithms 1-3) and clear mathematical formulations of watermark admissibility constraints.
The empirical evaluation explores multiple relevant dimensions—collection size, fine-tuning set size, and multi-watermark concurrent scaling—across two distinct open LLM architectures.
weaknesses: The approach is extremely fragile against standard LLM data-cleaning pipelines. Real-world web crawlers and curated dataset preparation pipelines (e.g., FineWeb, Dolma, RedPajama) routinely sanitize or strip non-printable/zero-width Unicode characters (U+200B, U+200C, U+200D, U+2060) as boilerplate or noise, which completely neutralizes the auditing mechanism before training occurs.

The experimental scope is restricted to LoRA fine-tuning on relatively small datasets (1k to 15k examples) over 3 epochs. Full fine-tuning, continued pretraining, instruction-tuning with structured chat templates, and RLHF are not evaluated, leaving the robustness of canary memorization in standard training regimes unverified.

Per-document detection power is low when the marked volume is small. As shown in Table II and Figure 2, detection relies on aggregating signals across dozens of watermarked documents (e.g., 30–50 documents), making the method ineffective for auditing single, isolated documents.

The framework relies heavily on a centralized Trusted Third Party (TTP) to ensure global cross-bifix-free properties and manage counterfactual sets across users, introducing significant coordination and operational overhead in real-world decentralized auditing scenarios.
